notes: \cpara{Summarizes the previous day's post, ``Asch's Conformity Experiment,'' in three findings: conformity, the effect of one dissenter, and the return of conformity when the dissenter sides with the group.}

\clogic{Asch at first read the result the same way: having had a partner ``had failed to strengthen the individuals' independence.'' He then traced the rise to the partner's ``desertion.'' When the partner simply left the room instead, ``the partner's effect outlasted his presence'' (1955). See the notes on the previous post.}
\cpara{States the benefits and costs of dissent in four short sentences. The rest of the post elaborates them.}
\cpara{The source of the post's ``sudden insight'' about how groups become overconfident: one conversation, told from the author's side.}

\cpara{Turns the anecdote into a general mechanism: politeness stops people from questioning each other's competence, so two doubters reassure each other into optimism. It is stated as general fact (``will have natural doubts,'' ``Together they become more optimistic''), with no support beyond the anecdote.}
\cpara{Extends the mechanism to whole groups and gives it its name.}

\cpara{Places the author and Robin Hanson in their debate on when to disagree, and says both accept a strong reading of Aumann's theorem. The footnoted post, ``The Modesty Argument'' (December 2006), gives the author's side of the debate: ``it can be rational for an individual to not adjust their own probability estimate in the direction of someone else who disagrees with them.'' The paragraph's last sentence reads as a mock rant; the next paragraph opens ``Ahem.''}

\clogic{The theorem assumes a common prior (see the notes on the previous post), and so does Hanson's own statement of the result: ``honest truth-seeking agents with common priors should not knowingly disagree'' (Cowen and Hanson, ``Are Disagreements Honest?''). To get ``someone must be irrational'' one needs the further claim that rational agents must share their priors, and that claim is disputed. Hanson's paper ``Uncommon Priors Require Origin Disputes,'' which ``The Modesty Argument'' cites, reports that some derive common priors from common knowledge of rationality, and that ``Others do not find this argument compelling''; Hanson argues for a version of the claim by another route. The post states the conclusion as agreed without the premise.}
\cpara{Draws the moral for rationalists: disagreeing with a group is ``serious business,'' not a matter of everyone's right to an opinion.}
\cpara{The lesson the post calls ``most important.'' Voicing a concern is not a promise to disagree at the end.}

\cpara{Says that ideal reasoners converge by sharing evidence the listener could not have predicted, and that this looks nothing like bargaining. Hanson's paper (\textsc{Economics Letters}, 2002, titled ``Disagreement is unpredictable'') shows that such agents ``cannot publicly anticipate the direction in which other agents will disagree with them.'' The link to the lesson is left implicit. My reading: a voiced concern is shared evidence, not a stated position.}

\cpara{Concedes that socially there is ``not much difference'' between a concern and a disagreement, that speaking out cannot be undone, and that the offended party ``will probably hold just as much of a grudge.'' This confines the lesson to groups that agree to honour the distinction, and the post says even they would be pretending.}
\cpara{Weighs both sides again: dissent inspires, conformity is powerful, the first to speak pays, and the distinction is ``a rationalist's artifice.''}
\cpara{Ends by leaving the decision to the reader. After naming the distinction as the ``most important lesson,'' the post gives no advice on when a concern is worth its cost.}
